idea: Two huge capitals, 'O.K.', with the small line 'oll korrect. Boston Morning Post, 23 March 1839.' The world's most used word began as a joke abbreviation from a newspaper fad for deliberate misspellings, so it's a shirt about how silly things win.

A dictionary entry set in a 1930s book face: 'dord (n.) Physics & Chem. Density.' Below it: 'Webster's, 1934 to 1947. This word never existed.' A slip meant to read 'D or d' (abbreviations for density) was printed as a word and stayed in the dictionary for years, which makes this a shirt for anyone who's ever had a mistake survive review.

A tidy encyclopedia entry: 'Mountweazel, Lillian Virginia (1942–1973). American photographer.' Underneath: 'She never lived. New Columbia Encyclopedia, 1975.' She was a fake entry planted to catch copiers, and the shirt is a deadpan nod to the traps hidden in reference books.

The SATOR square in five rows of Roman capitals: SATOR / AREPO / TENET / OPERA / ROTAS, captioned 'Reads the same four ways. Scratched on a wall in Pompeii before AD 79.' It's a 2,000-year-old word puzzle with perfect symmetry, so it works as pure pattern and as a deep cut.

The same line of type printed twice, labelled 'Baskerville' and 'Caslon', with the caption 'Franklin, 1760: a critic found faults in the "Baskerville". It was Caslon all along.' Benjamin Franklin wrote to John Baskerville about showing a Caslon specimen with its name cut off to a man who'd been complaining about Baskerville's type. It's a sharp point about how much we judge a label instead of the thing.

The single word 'honorificabilitudinitatibus' set in one long line across the chest, with 'Love's Labour's Lost, Act 5. Used once. 27 letters.' It's Shakespeare's longest word, said by the clown Costard, and the shirt is a love of language at its most showing-off.

A small sentence: 'Gadsby (1939): 50,000 words, and not a solitary word in it contains this glyph:' with one giant letter E below. Ernest Vincent Wright's novel really avoids the letter e, and the caption itself has none either, which readers enjoy finding out.

A line from Shakespeare in a fine old roman with several words neatly struck through, captioned 'bowdlerize (v.): after Thomas Bowdler, who cleaned up Shakespeare for families, 1807.' His Family Shakespeare cut whatever he thought improper, and his name became the word for it, which makes this a quietly anti-censorship shirt.

The real Maine law text set as a statute: '...packing for shipment or distribution of:' with a tiny caret marking where a comma isn't, captioned 'The missing comma cost a dairy $5 million. Maine, 2018.' In O'Connor v. Oakhurst Dairy, delivery drivers won overtime because of that ambiguity, and the case settled for $5 million. It's the serial-comma argument, settled by a court.

Two words, 'SHIBBOLETH' and 'sibboleth', with the second struck through, and 'Judges 12:6. Pronunciation as a password.' In the Bible story, the Gileadites caught fleeing Ephraimites because they couldn't say the 'sh', and the shirt points out that the way you talk has always been used to sort people.

One sentence set very large: 'The old man the boat.', and below in small type: 'Read it again.' It's a famous garden-path sentence, where 'man' is the verb and 'the old' are the crew, and the shirt is a small puzzle that makes people stop and think.

'Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo.' set as one sentence, with a tiny note: 'Grammatical. (Rapaport, 1972.)' Using the city, the animal and the verb 'to buffalo' (to bully), it's a real sentence, and a typographic in-joke for people who love the absurd parts of English.

A list of words that describe themselves: 'short', 'English', 'noun', 'polysyllabic', 'unhyphenated', headed 'Autological', and at the bottom: 'Is "heterological" heterological?' The question is the Grelling–Nelson paradox from 1908. It's a clean word list that ends in a logic trap.

A giant lowercase 'i' in a classic serif, with a fine leader line from its dot to one word, 'tittle.', and below: 'Not one jot or one tittle. Matthew 5:18.' The dot over an i really is called a tittle, and the shirt is for detail people who like the smallest marks having names.

'[sic]' set huge in square brackets, with 'Latin: thus. As in: they wrote it, not me.' Editors put it after a quoted error to show it's in the original, which makes it the politest putdown in print and a shirt for editors and pedants.

A library spine label with '001.9' and the Dewey heading below it: 'Controversial knowledge.' That really is the Dewey Decimal class for things like UFOs and the paranormal, so the shirt tells people how to shelve you.

The stage direction 'Exit, pursued by a bear.' set like a printed play, centred and italic, with 'The Winter's Tale, Act 3, Scene 3.' It's Shakespeare's most famous stage direction (Antigonus leaves and gets eaten), and it works as a dry exit line for anyone leaving a party early.

Strunk's rule set in a sober roman: 'Omit needless words.' with 'needless' crossed out by a proofreader's delete mark, so it reads 'Omit words.' Small caption: 'Strunk, 1918. Edited.' It's a joke for writers that also follows its own advice.

Pascal's line set as a short letter in a 17th-century French roman: 'Je n'ai fait celle-ci plus longue que parce que je n'ai pas eu le loisir de la faire plus courte.' with the translation 'I made this letter longer only because I had no time to make it shorter. Pascal, 1657.' It's the best case for editing ever written, from the Provincial Letters.

A justified column of text that runs off the bottom, with one short last line stranded alone at the top of the next column, labelled 'widow.', and the caption 'A paragraph's last line, alone on a new page. Typesetters fix these.' It's a type-nerd term turned into a quietly lonely image, and book designers will see the joke right away.
